sla_notes_intro: Garment construction is the process of making clothes from fabric using measuring, cutting, and sewing skills. Students learn its meaning, objectives and how a sewing room is organised.
sla_notes_details: Garment construction (tailoring, dressmaking) is the process of designing, drafting patterns, cutting, joining and finishing fabric pieces to produce wearable garments. Objectives: to provide skills for making, repairing and altering clothes, to save money, to develop creativity and self-employment, and to meet personal and family clothing needs. The sewing room should have good natural and artificial light, ventilation, enough space, a cutting table, machines, pressing area with iron and ironing board, storage shelves, a fitting corner with a mirror, and a first-aid kit. Basic equipment: measuring tools (tape measure, ruler, set square), marking tools (tailor's chalk, tracing wheel), cutting tools (shears, scissors, pinking shears), sewing tools (needles, pins, thimble, thread, seam ripper), and pressing tools. Safety and care: keep needles and pins in a pin cushion, unplug electric machines and iron when not in use, and keep the floor clear.
sla_notes_illustrations: A tailor's workshop in the market has a cutting table, two sewing machines, an iron, a mirror and shelves for fabric. Students draw the layout of a school sewing room and label each work area.
sla_notes_daily_life: Sewing skills allow you to mend school uniforms, make clothes for the family and start a tailoring business.
sla_exercise: Define garment construction.::Making clothes from fabric by measuring, cutting, sewing and finishing.||Name two cutting tools.::Shears and scissors (pinking shears).||Give two features of a good sewing room.::Good lighting and adequate space (ventilation, storage).

sla_notes_intro: The sewing machine joins fabric quickly and evenly. Students learn its parts, operation, common faults and care.
sla_notes_details: Types: hand-operated, treadle (foot-powered), electric and industrial. Main parts: spool pin, thread guide, tension discs, take-up lever, needle bar and needle, presser foot, feed dog, throat plate, bobbin and bobbin case, stitch length regulator, balance wheel and motor or pedal. Steps to sew: wind the bobbin, thread the upper thread through guides and needle, bring up the bobbin thread, place fabric under the presser foot, lower the foot and sew at an even speed, backstitch at the start and end. Adjust tension and stitch length for the fabric. Common faults and remedies: skipped stitches (bent or wrong needle), thread breaking (wrong tension or threading), puckering (tight tension), jamming (lint in bobbin case). Care: clean lint with a brush, oil moving parts regularly, cover after use, change blunt needles, and never sew over pins.
sla_notes_illustrations: If the upper thread keeps breaking, students rethread the machine with the presser foot raised, check the needle is inserted correctly and reduce the top tension.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing how to operate and maintain a machine saves repair costs and keeps it working for many years.
sla_exercise: Name two parts of a sewing machine.::Needle and presser foot (bobbin, feed dog).||Why oil a sewing machine?::To reduce friction and prevent wear of moving parts.||What may cause skipped stitches?::A bent, blunt or wrongly inserted needle.

sla_notes_intro: Garment making processes are the structural, decorative and functional techniques used to join and finish fabric. Students describe the rules for each.
sla_notes_details: Stitches: temporary (tacking, basting) and permanent (backstitch, running stitch, hemming, slip stitch, blanket stitch, overcasting). Seams: plain, French, flat-fell, double-stitched, and overlocked, chosen by fabric and garment. Openings: plackets, zips, slits, and continuous wrap openings, placed at side seams or centre back. Fasteners: buttons and buttonholes, hooks and eyes, press studs, zips, Velcro and ties. Disposal of fullness: darts, tucks, pleats, gathers and easing to shape flat fabric to body curves. Edge finishes: hems (turned, rolled), facings, binding, piping and overcasting to prevent fraying. Rules: press each seam, use the correct thread and needle, keep stitches even and finish neatly.
sla_notes_illustrations: A plain seam is made by placing two right sides together, stitching 1.5 cm from the edge, pressing open and neatening with zigzag or overcasting. It is used for side seams of a skirt.
sla_notes_daily_life: These techniques are used in everyday repairs such as sewing on buttons, fixing zips and hemming trousers.
sla_exercise: Name a temporary stitch.::Tacking (basting).||Give one method of disposing of fullness.::Darts, gathers, pleats or tucks.||What is the purpose of an edge finish?::To prevent fraying and give a neat appearance.

sla_notes_intro: A portfolio of prototypes is a folder of small fabric samples that show each technique. Students make prototypes of stitches, seams, openings, fastenings, fullness control and edge finishes.
sla_notes_details: Prototype (sample) making: cut fabric pieces about 15 by 10 cm, complete each technique step by step and mount neatly on manila card with a label giving the name, date, fabric and steps. Include sequences: hand stitches, machine seams (plain, French, flat-fell), an opening (zip or continuous wrap), fasteners (button and buttonhole, hook and eye, press stud), gathers, darts, tucks and pleats, and hems and facings. Presentation: order pages logically, keep samples clean and pressed, add a brief method note. Assessment considers accuracy, neatness, completeness and presentation.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student's page on French seam: stitch wrong sides together at 0.5 cm, trim, fold, stitch again 0.7 cm with right sides together, and label the steps beneath the sample.
sla_notes_daily_life: A portfolio serves as a reference guide for later sewing projects and a display of skills for customers or employers.
sla_exercise: What is a prototype?::A small sample showing how a technique is made.||Name one item to label on each sample.::The technique name, fabric or steps.||Why press samples before mounting?::So they look neat and flat.

sla_notes_intro: A pattern is a paper template used to cut fabric pieces accurately. Students take body measurements, draft, adapt, lay and cut out patterns for a skirt or pyjamas.
sla_notes_details: Body measurements are taken over light clothing with a tape measure held snug: waist, hip, skirt length, inside leg, crotch depth, bust, shoulder and arm length as required. For a basic straight skirt: rectangle width = quarter hip plus ease (about 2 cm), length = skirt length plus hem allowance; waist shaping is by darts (one to two on each half). Pyjama trousers: leg width from hip measurement plus ease, crotch curve and elastic waist casing. Adaptation adds features such as flare, pleats or pockets. Marks: grain line, notches, darts, centre front and fold. Layout: place pattern pieces on fabric along the grain, pin, and cut around leaving seam allowance of 1.5 cm and hem allowance of 4 cm. Label each piece with name and number of pieces to cut.
sla_notes_illustrations: For hip 92 cm the quarter measurement is 23 cm; adding 2 cm ease gives a skirt front and back width of 25 cm at the hips. The student draws it on brown paper.
sla_notes_daily_life: Making patterns lets you make well-fitting garments and cut fabric economically.
sla_exercise: Name two body measurements for a skirt.::Waist and hip (skirt length).||What is the seam allowance commonly used?::1.5 cm.||What does the grain line show?::The direction to place the pattern along the fabric threads.

sla_notes_intro: Assembling means joining cut pieces in the correct order to complete a garment. Students make a skirt or pyjamas.
sla_notes_details: Order for a skirt: mark and stitch darts, join side seams, insert zip at the opening, attach waistband or facing, hem, add a fastener and press. Order for pyjamas: neaten edges, join inside leg seams, join crotch seam, make the waistband casing, thread elastic, and hem the legs. At each step: press seams, check fit, and correct faults. Finishing: remove tacking, trim threads, press and inspect. Assessment: fit, seam quality, hem, zip, neatness and time management.
sla_notes_illustrations: A skirt is assembled by stitching darts (tapering to a point), joining side seams leaving the left side open for a zip, then attaching a waistband and turning the hem.
sla_notes_daily_life: Students gain the skill to make school uniforms and nightwear for the family.
sla_exercise: What is done first when assembling a skirt?::Mark and stitch the darts.||How is elastic inserted in pyjamas?::Threaded through a waistband casing.||Why press after each stage?::To keep seams flat and the garment neat.

sla_references: TET(2023), TEXTILES AND GARMENT CONSTRUCTION SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM I-IV, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Collars, cuffs, sleeves, pockets and other shaped parts give garments their style and function. Students describe the principles of making each.
sla_notes_details: Collars: flat (Peter Pan), rolled (shirt), stand (mandarin) and shawl; a collar has an upper and under piece with interfacing, joined at the neckline. Cuffs: plain, turn-back and buttoned. Sleeves: set-in, raglan, kimono and cap; sleeve heads are eased into the armhole. Pockets: patch, in-seam and slash. Facing: shaped fabric piece on the inside of edges (neckline, armhole) to finish and strengthen. Interfacing: stiff or fusible material between layers to give body to collars and cuffs. Lining: fabric inside a garment to hide seams and add comfort; interlining adds warmth. Ruffles, frills and trimmings (lace, braid, ribbon, bows) add decoration. Rules: grade seams, clip curves, press each stage and match notches.
sla_notes_illustrations: For a shirt collar: cut two collar pieces, apply fusible interfacing to one, sew them right sides together, trim, turn, press and top-stitch before attaching to the neckline.
sla_notes_daily_life: These processes are present in shirts, blouses and uniforms, and understanding them helps in choosing and repairing garments.
sla_exercise: What is the function of interfacing?::To give body and firmness to collars, cuffs and facings.||Name two types of pocket.::Patch and in-seam (slash) pocket.||Where is facing used?::On edges such as necklines and armholes.

sla_notes_details: Order for a blouse or shirt: stitch darts, join shoulder seams, prepare and attach the collar, make and set in sleeves, join side and underarm seams, make buttonholes and sew on buttons, and hem. For an apron: hem the edges, gather the skirt, attach the bib and waistband, add the pocket and ties. Quality checks: even stitching, symmetrical pieces, smooth curves, neat buttonholes, correct fit and pressed finish. Faults such as puckering, uneven hems and loose threads are corrected.

sla_notes_intro: Design is the plan of how a garment looks. Students study the elements (line, shape, colour, texture, space) and principles (balance, emphasis, alignment) used to create attractive garments.
sla_notes_details: Elements: line (vertical lines lengthen, horizontal lines widen, curved lines soften), shape or silhouette (A-line, straight, flared), space (area within and around the garment), colour (hue, value, intensity, colour schemes such as monochromatic, complementary, analogous), and texture (smooth, rough, shiny, crisp). Principles: balance (formal or symmetrical, informal or asymmetrical), emphasis (a focal point such as a collar or embroidery), rhythm, proportion, harmony and alignment (arrangement of parts along a straight or grain line). A good design suits the wearer's figure, age, occasion, fabric and skill of the maker.
sla_notes_illustrations: A blouse with a bright embroidered collar on a plain fabric creates emphasis, while vertical stripes and a centre front opening create a long, slim line.
sla_notes_daily_life: Applying design principles helps you dress attractively and make garments that customers like.
sla_exercise: Name two elements of design.::Line and colour (shape, texture).||What effect do vertical lines give?::They make the wearer look taller and slimmer.||What is emphasis?::A focal point that attracts attention in the design.

sla_notes_intro: Body shape, size and proportions affect how fabric patterns, lines, colours and textures look on a person. Students analyse these effects.
sla_notes_details: Figure types: tall and slim, short, heavy or full figure, pear (broad hips) and inverted triangle (broad shoulders). Choices: slim figures suit horizontal lines, bright colours, bulky or textured fabrics and gathers; full figures suit vertical lines, dark colours, smooth fabrics with soft drape and small prints; short figures suit small patterns and one-colour outfits; tall figures suit large prints and horizontal patterns. Fabric texture: stiff fabrics add volume, soft fabrics cling. Colour: light adds size and dark reduces it. Consider skin tone and occasion.
sla_notes_illustrations: A heavy woman choosing fabric for a dress should prefer a plain dark fabric with a soft drape and vertical seams instead of a large bright check.
sla_notes_daily_life: Choosing fabric to suit your figure improves your appearance and confidence and avoids wasted purchases.
sla_exercise: Which line effect suits a full figure?::Vertical lines.||What do dark colours do?::They make the figure look smaller.||Give a fabric suggestion for a slim figure.::Textured or bulky fabrics with horizontal lines.

sla_notes_intro: Students prepare patterns for a dress, a pair of shorts or trousers from body measurements.
sla_notes_details: Measurements for a dress: bust, waist, hip, shoulder, dress length, sleeve length, back length. For trousers or shorts: waist, hip, crotch depth, thigh, inside leg, length and knee. Draft basic blocks; bodice with bust darts and skirt with waist darts joined at waist for a dress; trouser block with front and back crotch curves, dart and fly. Adapt: shape the neckline, sleeves, pleats, pockets and waistband. Add notches and grain lines, seam allowance 1.5 cm, hem 4 cm. Test the pattern with a toile (calico) to check fit before cutting the fabric. Lay patterns economically, cut with sharp shears and transfer marks.
sla_notes_illustrations: For trousers with hip 100 cm: hip line width at half the pattern is quarter hip (25 cm) plus 2.5 cm ease; crotch depth is measured from waist to seat when sitting.
sla_notes_daily_life: Well-drafted patterns are the base of custom tailoring and help avoid costly cutting errors.

sla_notes_intro: Students make a complete garment: a dress, shorts or trousers, using processes learned.
sla_notes_details: Dress: stitch darts, join shoulder and side seams, insert zip, set in sleeves, attach collar or facing, join skirt to bodice, and hem. Shorts and trousers: stitch darts and pockets, join centre seams, insert fly zip, make the waistband, join inside leg seams, hem and add fasteners. At each stage check fit, press seams and finish edges. Faults and remedies: pulling at the seat (need more ease), gaping waist (add dart or elastic), crooked hem (level with a ruler). Assessment: fit, workmanship, finishing, time and cost of materials.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student makes shorts: sews front and back darts, attaches side pockets, joins crotch seams, sews the waistband with elastic and hems the legs.
sla_notes_daily_life: Being able to make and alter dresses and trousers reduces clothing costs and supports tailoring as a career.

sla_notes_intro: Caring for clothes keeps them clean, in good condition and long lasting. Students describe daily, routine and preventative care.
sla_notes_details: Daily care: hang garments after wearing, brush off dust, air them, and change stained items. Routine care: washing (hand or machine), sorting by colour and fibre, following care labels, drying, ironing at a temperature suited to the fibre, folding or storing on hangers, dry-cleaning where needed. Preventative care: mending small tears and loose buttons promptly, removing stains quickly, storing with moth repellents in dry cupboards, avoiding overloading wardrobes and using proper hangers. Stain removal: rinse blood in cold water, use lemon and salt for rust or ink, absorbents for grease. Labels use symbols for washing, bleaching, ironing and drying.
sla_notes_illustrations: A cotton school shirt is soaked, scrubbed with soap, rinsed, dried in shade, ironed while slightly damp and hung. A missing button is sewn on before the next wear.
sla_notes_daily_life: Good clothing care saves money and keeps a neat appearance at school and at work.
sla_exercise: Why sort clothes before washing?::To prevent colours running and to treat fibres properly.||Give one preventative care practice.::Mending small tears at once (or storing with moth repellent).||What do care label symbols show?::How to wash, dry, iron and bleach the garment.

sla_notes_intro: Decorative processes add beauty and value to garments. Students describe the principles for making appliqué, scallops, smocking, faggoting, piping and binding.
sla_notes_details: Applique: sewing shaped fabric pieces onto a base fabric by hand or machine using satin stitch or blanket stitch. Scallops: curved edges made by marking, stitching and clipping a facing. Smocking: gathering fabric in even rows and embroidering over the folds in honeycomb or cable patterns; suited to children's dresses. Faggoting: joining two folded edges with decorative stitches leaving an open gap. Piping: a fabric-covered cord inserted in a seam to give a raised edge. Binding: a bias strip enclosing raw edges. Principles: keep decoration in proportion to the garment, place at focal points, use suitable colours and threads, and keep stitches even.
sla_notes_illustrations: To pipe a cushion or collar: cut bias strips, cover a cord, tack it between the fabric layers with the seam line and stitch close to the cord.
sla_notes_daily_life: Decorative skills are used in making children's dresses, cushions and gifts and can be sold for income.
sla_exercise: What is smocking?::Decoration made by gathering fabric and embroidering over the gathers.||Name one use of bias binding.::Enclosing raw edges neatly.||Which process gives a raised seam edge?::Piping.

sla_notes_intro: Students make samples of embroidery stitches, appliqué, scallops, smocking, faggoting, piping and binding suited to children's clothes.
sla_notes_details: Prototypes: embroidery stitches (chain, stem, satin, lazy daisy, French knot), applique shapes such as animals and flowers, scalloped edges, honeycomb smocking, faggoting between two hems, piped seams and bias-bound edges. Each sample is neat, on suitable fabric, pressed and mounted with labels. Choose designs safe for children: no loose buttons or sharp ornaments, soft fabrics and washable materials.
sla_notes_illustrations: A page shows a lazy daisy flower embroidered on a cotton square with steps: mark, hoop, make loop stitches in a circle and add a French knot in the centre.
sla_notes_daily_life: These samples serve as a guide for decorating children's dresses and for orders from clients.

sla_notes_intro: Children's clothes should be comfortable, safe and durable. Students discuss the factors that influence fabric choice.
sla_notes_details: Factors: comfort (soft, absorbent fabrics such as cotton for skin contact), safety (flame-resistant, no small detachable trims), durability (strong weave that withstands play and frequent washing), ease of care (washable, colour-fast, quick-drying, non-iron), growth (allow room and hems that can be let down), climate and season, cost, colour and design (bright, cheerful), age and gender, skin sensitivity, and fabric width and quantity. For babies choose soft, light, pale cotton or flannelette; for schoolchildren choose hardwearing polyester-cotton blends.
sla_notes_illustrations: A mother choosing fabric for a baby's dress selects soft white cotton because it is absorbent, safe on skin and easy to wash.
sla_notes_daily_life: Right fabric choices keep children comfortable and reduce clothing costs.
sla_exercise: Give two factors in choosing children's fabric.::Comfort and durability (washability, safety).||Which fibre is best for a baby's skin?::Soft cotton.||Why allow for growth?::Children grow quickly so garments should last longer.

sla_notes_intro: Students take a child's measurements and draft a pattern suitable for a child's garment such as a dress or shorts.
sla_notes_details: Child measurements: chest, waist, hip, shoulder, back length, sleeve length and garment length; take them with the child standing straight, and add extra ease for movement. Children have less waist definition, so patterns are looser with elastic waists and easy openings for dressing. Draft a simple dress block with round neck, short sleeves and gathers; add features such as pockets, smocked yoke or frills. Allow for growth with generous hems and adjustable straps. Cut, mark and lay economically.
sla_notes_illustrations: For a girl of age 5 with chest 56 cm, the front bodice width is a quarter of chest plus 4 cm ease, i.e. 18 cm, and the pattern includes a 5 cm hem allowance.
sla_notes_daily_life: Making children's clothes at home is cheaper and can be tailored to the child's comfort.
sla_exercise: Why add extra ease in children's patterns?::To allow free movement and growth.||Give one feature for easy dressing.::Elastic waist or wide neck opening.||Which measurement is needed for a child's dress?::Chest and dress length (shoulder, waist).

sla_notes_intro: Students design and complete a child's garment applying decorative techniques such as smocking, appliqué and piping.
sla_notes_details: Process: sketch the design, choose fabric and trims, cut, decorate sections before assembly (smock the yoke, applique the pocket), assemble the garment, and add finishing touches such as piped edges or binding. Practical tips: prepare embroidery threads and needles, use an embroidery hoop, test decorations on scraps, and place decorations symmetrically. Safety and quality: firm stitching so ornaments do not come off, smooth inside seams for comfort. Evaluate creativity, workmanship, fit, suitability and finishing.
sla_notes_illustrations: A pupil makes a girl's sundress with a smocked bodice, appliqued flower pocket, bias-bound armholes and a hem trimmed with lace.
sla_notes_daily_life: Decorated children's garments sell well and can be a source of income for a tailor.
sla_exercise: When is smocking done in garment construction?::Before assembling the garment sections.||Why test decorations on scraps?::To check the stitch and look before working on the garment.||Name one criterion for evaluating the garment.::Workmanship, fit or creativity.

sla_notes_intro: A wardrobe plan helps a person organise and budget for clothing. Students develop a plan with an inventory and a chart.
sla_notes_details: A personal wardrobe is the collection of clothes and accessories a person owns. Wardrobe inventory: list each garment, its condition, colour, occasion and whether it needs repair, then identify gaps and unused items. Wardrobe plan: consider lifestyle, occasions, climate, budget, figure and colour palette; choose basic pieces that mix and match, decide what to buy, make, repair or discard, and set priorities. Chart columns: item, colour, use, condition, action and estimated cost. Benefits: reduces impulse buying, saves money and gives a coordinated look.
sla_notes_illustrations: A student lists 3 shirts, 2 trousers, 1 skirt and 1 pair of school shoes, sees a need for a formal dress, and plans to sew it during the holiday, estimating the fabric cost.
sla_notes_daily_life: Planning a wardrobe helps you spend wisely and always be well dressed.
sla_exercise: Define a wardrobe inventory.::A list of the clothes a person owns and their condition.||Give one benefit of a wardrobe plan.::Saves money (avoids impulse buying).||Name a column in a wardrobe chart.::Item, colour, condition or cost.

sla_notes_intro: Professionalism means behaving responsibly and skilfully in a trade. Students describe the basic elements of professionalism, ethics and customer care in tailoring.
sla_notes_details: Professionalism: competence, punctuality, honesty, neat appearance, keeping records, continuous learning and respect for laws such as licensing and tax. Ethics: fairness in pricing, keeping promises on delivery dates, confidentiality of customer measurements and designs, not copying without permission, proper use of fabric supplied by customers, and safety. Customer care: greet politely, listen to needs, take accurate measurements, advise on styles and fabrics, quote a clear price and date, hold fittings, handle complaints calmly, and follow up after delivery. Good service builds trust and repeat business.
sla_notes_illustrations: A customer brings fabric for a dress; the tailor records measurements and delivery date, informs her of the cost, returns the leftover fabric and invites her to a fitting.
sla_notes_daily_life: Ethical behaviour and good customer care are essential to running a successful tailoring business.
